t: What regulators said. What marketing says.
x: Official warnings, the selling tricks that come up again and again, and claims that do not survive contact with the research. Tirzepatide recall from compounding pharmacy Apothecary Pharma (US), 24 Sep 2026 Apothecary Pharma LLC of Cary, North Carolina, a compounding pharmacy (not the maker of Mounjaro or Zepbound), voluntarily recalled its tirzepatide injection 18 mg/mL and an NAD+ injection across the US. The reason in the FDA enforcement report: lack of assurance of sterility. The FDA classified the recall as Class II, meaning the product may cause temporary or medically reversible health effects, with serious problems unlikely. Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. Anyone who has this product should contact their doctor; the lot numbers are listed in the FDA report. FDA warning letters to peptide sellers The FDA sends warning letters when it decides a firm is selling unapproved drugs. In several cases the agency stated plainly that a “for research purposes only” label changes nothing, and it treated website claims, guides, calculators and bacteriostatic water sold alongside as evidence the products were meant for people. Counterfeit Ozempic in the legitimate supply chain The FDA warned three times about counterfeit Ozempic 1 mg that reached the normal US supply: lots NAR0074 (December 2023), PAR0362 (April 2025) and PAR1229 (December 2025). In the first batch the needles were counterfeit too, so sterility could not be confirmed. Salt forms instead of the active ingredient The FDA states that “semaglutide sodium” and “semaglutide acetate” are different active ingredients from semaglutide and that it is not aware of any lawful basis for using them. It also warns about products falsely labelled “for research” or “not for human consumption” sold straight to consumers. What was actually in products bought online In a study published in JAMA Network Open, semaglutide was test-purchased from six no-prescription vendors. Three orders never arrived. In the three that did, purity was 7 to 14 percent against an advertised 99, and content was 29 to 39 percent above the label. An independent analysis of melanotan II found 4.3 to 8.8 mg of peptide in vials labelled 10 mg. How to check this yourself The FDA runs an open database of products subject to recalls and warnings. You type a name and see the date, the firm, what the violation was and what action was taken. The agency itself notes the database covers only a fraction of the products on the market, so absence from it does not mean something is safe. “For research purposes only” A formula meant to shift responsibility onto the buyer. It is not a legal category that protects a seller: the FDA judged intended use by what the firm writes and what it sells alongside. A certificate that certifies nothing A scanned document with no laboratory name, date, batch number or method. The same file gets reused across sellers and batches. Before-and-after photos Lighting, time of day, hydration and muscle tension change appearance more than most substances do. Such photos prove nothing. A list of twenty effects The longer the list of promises, the weaker the evidence. It usually comes from cell or animal studies, at doses and routes that do not translate to people. A study that is not about the product A seller links a real paper, but it covers a different substance, a different form or only cells. It is worth opening the link and reading who was studied. Urgency and limits Countdown timers, “last units”, a discount only today. A sales device, not information about quality. Faceless reviews Reviews on a seller’s site are moderated by that seller. There is no way to know who wrote them or whether anyone received the same product. Vocabulary that dodges the law “Not for human consumption”, “reference material”, “reagent”. The wording changes the description, not what is inside or who it is sold to. Myth Research peptides bought online are the same as pharmacy medicines. “Research only” products do not have to meet the sterility, purity and dose-accuracy standards that apply to medicines. Vial contents may differ from the label, and batches are usually not independently checked. Myth If it is a natural peptide, it is safe. Insulin, glucagon and vasopressin are natural too, and the wrong dose can kill. Safety depends on dose, purity, route and human studies, not on where the molecule comes from. Myth BPC-157 is well studied in humans. A 2025 review found only 3 small human studies, under 30 people in total, without control groups. Almost all data come from animal studies. Myth In 2026 the FDA approved BPC-157 and TB-500. In July 2026 an FDA advisory committee only recommended adding them to the list of compounding ingredients (8 to 6). That is a non-binding recommendation, not drug approval, and it does not cover products from online shops. Myth Two GLP-1 drugs at once means faster weight loss. They act on the same receptor, so mainly side effects add up: nausea, vomiting, dehydration. The maker of tirzepatide states there are no data on combining it with other GLP-1 agonists. Myth After stopping an obesity drug the weight stays off. In withdrawal trials (STEP 4 for semaglutide, SURMOUNT-4 for tirzepatide) a large part of the lost weight returned within a year. These drugs work while they are taken. Partly true A peptide pill works just like an injection. Most peptides are digested in the stomach and gut. Exceptions such as oral semaglutide use a special absorption enhancer, need much higher doses and must be taken on an empty stomach. Partly true Collagen powder rebuilds your skin. A 2023 meta-analysis of 26 trials found a modest improvement in skin elasticity and hydration. Trials were small, some results subjective, and it does not replace sun protection. Partly true A certificate of analysis (CoA) guarantees quality. A CoA shows the result for one sample. If the seller issued it, without an independent lab and a batch number matching the package, it proves little. It does not replace sterility testing or drug-grade control. Myth Peptide cream works like Botox. Botulinum toxin is injected and blocks nerves in the muscle. Peptides in creams barely cross the epidermis, and evidence comes mostly from lab work and small manufacturer studies. Worth checking GLP-1 drugs are approved only for diabetes. Not true the other way round: several (Wegovy, Zepbound, Saxenda, and since 2026 the Foundayo pill) are separately approved for obesity, and Wegovy also for cardiovascular risk reduction. They are still prescription drugs under medical supervision.

17 questions about peptides, answered from the research — and about what we will not answer. Are peptides proteins? Peptides and proteins are made of the same amino acids. Peptides are shorter, proteins longer and folded into a stable structure. The border is conventional, often around 50 amino acids. Do peptides in creams reach the deeper skin? It depends on the molecule and carrier. Large molecules cross the epidermis poorly, so makers modify peptides, for example by attaching a fatty acid. Much of the data comes from lab studies. Why are peptide drugs usually injected? Peptides are digested by gut acid and enzymes, trapped by mucus and cross the gut lining poorly. An exception is semaglutide tablets, approved in 2019, which work with an absorption enhancer. Are peptides bought online safe? “Research only” products are not controlled like drugs and human data on them are scarce. Details are in the blog article. Does collagen powder work? A 2023 meta-analysis points to a modest gain in skin elasticity and hydration in healthy adults, but trials were small and partly subjective. It does not replace treatment. Where can I buy peptides? Approved peptide drugs are available only by prescription, from a pharmacy, after a doctor's decision. Substances sold as “research only” are not medicines: they lack drug-grade quality control and are not approved for human use. This site lists no shops, links or prices for peptides. How are lyophilized peptides stored? General rule for lyophilized powders: cool, dry, tightly sealed, away from light and moisture. After reconstitution peptides are usually much less stable. For a medicine, the exact conditions are in its leaflet, not in general rules. What is the difference between purity and peptide content? Purity (e.g. by HPLC) tells what share of the peptide material is the target peptide rather than related peptides. Peptide content tells what share of the vial mass is peptide at all, the rest being salts, water and excipients. High purity therefore does not mean the labelled mass is all active substance. How do I read a certificate of analysis (CoA)? Check: name and batch number matching the package, date, method (HPLC for purity, mass spectrometry for identity), result and who tested. A certificate issued by the seller without an independent lab proves little, and a CoA neither makes a substance a medicine nor replaces quality control. Can I ask about a dose or how to use something? We do not answer those. For most substances in the catalog no safe human dose has been established, and the numbers circulating on forums and from sellers are guesswork. We give doses only for approved drugs, copied from current labels, in the Dosing tab. Which seller is trustworthy? We do not recommend sellers and we do not run rankings. “Research” products are not medicines and nobody checks their contents or sterility. The Alerts tab collects FDA documents and studies showing what such products contain. What does “for research purposes only” mean? To the FDA, nothing. In warning letters the agency stated plainly that such a label does not change a product’s status when everything around it shows it is meant for people: effect claims, guides, calculators or bacteriostatic water sold alongside. I have a worrying symptom after a peptide. What should I do? We cannot assess symptoms over a message and we do not replace a doctor. For severe or sudden symptoms call emergency services. Tell the doctor exactly what was taken and when, even if it came from the internet. You can also describe the symptom in our form; reports are not published. Does a certificate of analysis (COA) mean a product is safe? No. A COA describes one sample, not a whole batch, and says nothing about sterility or whether the tested sample came from what you receive. Such documents also get copied between sellers. Independent analyses of products bought online found purity in the low tens of percent against an advertised 99. Is peptide X banned in sport? Check the anti-doping checker in the Catalog tab. It shows the WADA class and whether the ban applies at all times. Watch for the S0 clause: it covers substances with no approval for human treatment, even when they are not named. Why don’t you say something works when people say it helped them? Because individual reports cannot separate a substance’s effect from time, rehabilitation, a change in training or placebo. That is why each entry shows how many human trials are actually registered, with sources so anyone can check. Can I advertise my product here? No. We do not work with peptide sellers and we do not publish ads or shop links. The catalog is free and funded by our optional PDF guides, with no commission from anyone.

Terms that come up on every page, explained once so the rest of the site reads easily. "Research use only" A label on products sold as laboratory reagents. It means the product is not a medicine and has not passed the quality and sterility checks required for medicines. Adverse effect A harmful or unwanted effect of a medicine or substance. Trials record all such events, including ones not proven to be caused by the substance. Agonist A substance that activates a receptor the way a natural signal does. Amino acid A building block of peptides and proteins. The body uses 20 standard ones. Analog A substance similar to a natural molecule, chemically modified, often to last longer. Antagonist A substance that blocks a receptor without activating it. Approved drug A substance authorised by a regulator (e.g. FDA, EMA) for a stated use. Bioavailability The share of a substance that reaches the blood in active form. Most peptides have very low bioavailability when swallowed, because enzymes digest them. Certificate of analysis (COA) A document with test results for a product batch. Its value depends on who tested it and how; a certificate issued by the seller itself proves little. Clinical trial phase Stages of testing a medicine in people. Phase 1: safety in a small group. Phase 2: whether it works and at what amount. Phase 3: large comparative trials before approval. Phase 4: monitoring after it reaches the market. Compounded drug A medicine prepared by a pharmacy for a specific patient rather than made in a factory. In the US, compounded drugs are not reviewed by the FDA like standard medicines. Concentration Mass of substance divided by solution volume, e.g. mg/ml. Control group Study participants who do not get the tested substance (they get placebo or standard care). Without one, it is impossible to tell whether an improvement came from the substance. DEXA A low-dose X-ray scan of body composition. It measures fat, lean mass and bone; shifts in water and glycogen can exaggerate short-term lean-mass loss. Double-blind A study in which neither participants nor researchers know who gets the medicine and who gets placebo. This reduces the influence of expectations on the results. Dual and triple agonist A molecule that activates two (for example GLP-1 and GIP) or three (GLP-1, GIP and glucagon) different receptors at once. More receptors can mean a stronger effect, but also more unknowns about safety. Endotoxin A fragment of the bacterial cell wall that can cause fever and inflammation even after the bacteria are dead. Medicines are tested for endotoxins; "research" products often are not. GIP The second incretin hormone from the gut (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide). It boosts insulin release after meals. Tirzepatide acts on both GIP and GLP-1 receptors. GLP-1 A gut hormone (glucagon-like peptide-1) released after meals. It raises glucose-dependent insulin release, slows stomach emptying and reduces appetite. Natural GLP-1 breaks down within minutes, so medicines use longer-lasting analogues. Glucagon A pancreatic hormone that raises blood glucose and increases energy use by the liver. Retatrutide and survodutide also act on the glucagon receptor, which is meant to raise energy expenditure. Growth hormone secretagogue A substance that prompts the pituitary gland to release growth hormone. This group includes GHRH analogues and ghrelin mimetics. Half-life Time for the blood concentration of a substance to fall by half. IGF-1 Insulin-like growth factor 1, made mainly by the liver in response to growth hormone. It carries out many of growth hormone's effects; its level is used to assess the growth hormone axis. Incretins Gut hormones that increase insulin release after a meal. The main ones are GLP-1 and GIP. Incretin medicines mimic their action. Indication The disease or condition a medicine is approved for. Off-label use has not been assessed by the regulator for that purpose. Lean mass Everything in the body except fat: muscle, organs, bone and water. With fast weight loss, part of the weight lost is lean mass. Lyophilizate A substance freeze-dried under vacuum and supplied as a powder in a vial. Melanocortins A group of hormones and receptors (MC1R–MC5R) that affect skin pigmentation, appetite and sexual function, among others. Afamelanotide and bremelanotide act on them. Meta-analysis An analysis that combines the results of many studies on the same question. It gives a stronger conclusion than one study, provided the studies were of good quality. Off-label Using an approved medicine for a different condition, amount or patient group than its label states. Doctors may prescribe this way, but the evidence is often weaker. Overdose Taking more than is safe. Symptoms need urgent help. Peptide A short chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Usually up to about 50 residues; longer chains are proteins. Placebo An inactive substance given to a control group to separate the real effect of a medicine from expectation and chance. Studies without placebo or a control group give weak evidence. Preclinical study Research in cells or animals before a substance is tested in people. Most results at this stage are not confirmed later in humans. Prescribing information (label) The official document for a medicine approved by a regulator: uses, dosing, contraindications and side effects. In the US it is the label on DailyMed; in the EU and UK it is the SmPC. Purity (HPLC) The percentage of a sample made up of one compound, measured by chromatography. High purity does not say whether it is the right compound; that needs an identity test such as mass spectrometry. RCT Randomised controlled trial with a control group (placebo). Usually the strongest evidence of effect. Receptor A protein on or inside a cell that a specific molecule fits like a key in a lock. Binding triggers a specific response in the cell. Reconstitution Dissolving the powder in a solvent before use. It changes concentration, not the amount of substance. Regulators (FDA, EMA, MHRA) Agencies that approve medicines: the FDA in the US, the EMA in the European Union and the MHRA in the UK. Approval in one country does not mean approval in another. Sterility The absence of living microorganisms in a product. It is required for medicines given by routes that bypass the gut; without it there is a risk of infection. Systematic review A structured collection of all studies on a topic, gathered by set rules. It shows how much is known and how strong the evidence is. Tachyphylaxis A rapid loss of effect when the same substance is given repeatedly. It affects, for example, some growth-hormone-releasing peptides. WADA World Anti-Doping Agency. Publishes the list of substances banned in sport. WADA S0 list The WADA Prohibited List category for substances not approved for human use. It covers many peptides sold "for research".

Vasopressin 2026-10-25 Vasopressin is a peptide hormone of nine amino acids, made in the hypothalamus and released from the pituitary gland. It binds V1 and V2 receptors: it narrows blood vessels and makes the kidneys hold on to water, which is why it is also called the antidiuretic hormone. It is an approved medicine for vasodilatory shock and is given only in a healthcare setting. Its structure was worked out and synthesised by Vincent du Vigneaud's group, which earned him the 1955 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work on peptide hormones. Who we are PepSafe (pepsafe.info) is an independent educational website about peptides and GLP-1 medicines. Contact: contact@pepsafe.info. What we collect If you join our email list, we collect your email address and the date of your consent. If you use the contact or side-effect form, we collect what you type into it. We do not ask for health records and you should not send them. Why To send you the weekly PepSafe email and the free checklist (legal basis: your consent), and to answer messages you send us. Who processes it Forms are delivered to our inbox by FormSubmit (formsubmit.co). Our email list is hosted by MailerLite (UAB MailerLite, Lithuania, EU), which stores your email address and consent date and sends our emails on our behalf. Purchases on Ko-fi are handled by Ko-fi and PayPal/Stripe under their own privacy policies; we receive only what they share with sellers. Side-effect reports The side-effect form collects health information (special category data). We process it only with your explicit consent, given with the checkbox on the form, only to read the report and notice repeated safety problems. It is sent by FormSubmit to our inbox, read only by the site authors, never published, never shared and never used for marketing. Do not include your name, contact details or medical records. We delete reports within 12 months; you can ask us to delete yours earlier at contact@pepsafe.info. We do not forward reports to regulators: to report officially, use the MHRA Yellow Card (UK) or FDA MedWatch (US). Analytics We count visits with Cloudflare Web Analytics, which does not use cookies and does not track you across websites. How long We keep your email until you unsubscribe or ask us to delete it. Messages are kept only as long as needed to reply. Your rights You can unsubscribe at any time with the link in every email, or ask us to see, correct or delete your data by writing to contact@pepsafe.info. UK residents can complain to the Information Commissioner's Office (ico.org.uk). No sales of data We never sell or rent your data, and we do not sell medicines or peptides. Last updated: October 2026.

How Liraglutide and Exenatide differ: approval status, how they work, what the research shows and what to watch for. Facts from the catalog, with sources. Status Liraglutide: Approved drug Exenatide: Approved drug What it is Liraglutide: An older GLP-1 agonist given daily. Its longer action comes from an attached fatty acid. Exenatide: The first approved GLP-1 agonist (2005). Derived from exendin-4, a peptide from Gila monster saliva. How it works Liraglutide: Binds the GLP-1 receptor like semaglutide but acts for a shorter time. Exenatide: Binds the GLP-1 receptor and increases insulin release after meals. Use Liraglutide: Type 2 diabetes (Victoza), obesity treatment (Saxenda). Exenatide: Type 2 diabetes. What the research shows Liraglutide: Phase 3 trials, many years of clinical experience. Exenatide: Phase 3 trials, long experience. What to watch for Liraglutide: Do not combine with other GLP-1 agonists or tirzepatide. Hypoglycemia with insulin or a sulfonylurea. Exenatide: Do not combine with other GLP-1 agonists or tirzepatide. Hypoglycemia with insulin or a sulfonylurea. How Retatrutide and Survodutide differ: approval status, how they work, what the research shows and what to watch for. Facts from the catalog, with sources. Status Retatrutide: In clinical trials Survodutide: In clinical trials What it is Retatrutide: An experimental Eli Lilly peptide given once weekly. It adds the glucagon receptor to tirzepatide's action. Survodutide: A Boehringer Ingelheim peptide in clinical trials. How it works Retatrutide: Activates three receptors: GIP and GLP-1 (insulin, appetite) and glucagon (energy expenditure and liver metabolism). Survodutide: Activates GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. Use Retatrutide: Studied in: obesity, type 2 diabetes, knee osteoarthritis pain, sleep apnea, fatty liver disease. Survodutide: Studied in: obesity and fatty liver disease. What the research shows Retatrutide: Phase 3 results announced by the maker in 2025–2026 (weight and A1C reduction). Not approved; the maker plans to file in 2027. Survodutide: Phase 3, not approved. What to watch for Retatrutide: Do not combine with tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound), semaglutide or other GLP-1 agonists: double action on the same receptors, no data. Products sold as retatrutide outside trials do not come from the drug's maker. Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and constipation were common in trials. Survodutide: Do not combine with other GLP-1 agonists. There are no studied combinations with medicines or other peptides. Combining them is a doctor's decision. Status Semaglutide: Approved drug Cagrilintide: In clinical trials What it is Semaglutide: A chemically modified peptide similar to human GLP-1, with additions that prolong its action. How it works Semaglutide: Binds the GLP-1 receptor: increases glucose-dependent insulin release, slows stomach emptying and reduces appetite through the brain. Cagrilintide: Mimics amylin, a satiety hormone released together with insulin. Use Semaglutide: Type 2 diabetes, obesity treatment, cardiovascular risk reduction (depending on product). Cagrilintide: Studied in: obesity. What the research shows Semaglutide: Large phase 3 trials and regulatory approvals. Cagrilintide: Phase 3; an application for CagriSema has been filed. Cagrilintide: The combination with semaglutide is studied in fixed proportions. Mixing it yourself with other products is not the same and there are no data. t: Amino acid, peptide, protein: what is the difference
x: Amino acids are the building blocks. Humans use 20 standard amino acids, each with an amino and a carboxyl group. When the carboxyl group of one joins the amino group of the next, a peptide bond forms and a molecule of water is released. Two amino acids make a dipeptide, three a tripeptide, and chains up to about 20 are called oligopeptides. Longer ones are polypeptides. The line between a long peptide and a protein is conventional. Often about 50 amino acids is used, or whether the chain folds into a stable structure on its own. Insulin shows how blurry the line is: it has 51 amino acids in two chains and is called both a peptide hormone and a small protein. t: Collagen powder: what the studies show
x: Hydrolyzed collagen is collagen broken by enzymes into short peptides. In the gut it is digested further into amino acids and di- and tripeptides, and some short fragments have been detected in blood after eating. A 2023 meta-analysis by Pu and colleagues covered 26 randomized trials and 1,721 healthy adults taking collagen for 2 to 12 weeks. It found better skin elasticity and hydration than placebo, with larger effects after more than 8 weeks. There are limits: trials were small, some elasticity measures were self-reported, and most used marine collagen. Collagen will not replace sun protection or treatment of skin disease. t: GLP-1 weight-loss medicines: a guide to semaglutide, tirzepatide and retatrutide
x: Key takeaways: semaglutide and tirzepatide are approved medicines; retatrutide is still in trials and approved nowhere. In the main trials, average weight loss was about 15% with semaglutide (68 weeks), about 21% with tirzepatide (72 weeks) and about 24% with retatrutide (48 weeks, phase 2). Side effects are mostly digestive. Much of the weight tends to come back after stopping. Products sold online as "research" versions are not the trial medicines. How they work. GLP-1 is a gut hormone released after meals. It increases insulin release when glucose is high, slows stomach emptying and reduces appetite through the brain. Natural GLP-1 lasts only minutes, so the medicines are modified versions that last about a week. Liraglutide (daily) and semaglutide (weekly) act on the GLP-1 receptor only. Tirzepatide adds a second receptor, GIP. Retatrutide adds a third, the glucagon receptor, which is meant to increase energy use. What the trials showed. In STEP 1 (NEJM 2021), adults with obesity on semaglutide lost on average 14.9% of body weight over 68 weeks, compared with 2.4% on placebo. In SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM 2022), tirzepatide at the highest level tested led to an average loss of 20.9% over 72 weeks, versus 3.1% on placebo. In a phase 2 trial of retatrutide (NEJM 2023), the highest level tested led to an average loss of 24.2% over 48 weeks. These are averages: some people lost much more, some much less. Approval status. Semaglutide is approved for weight management (Wegovy) and type 2 diabetes (Ozempic, Rybelsus). Tirzepatide is approved for weight management (Zepbound) and type 2 diabetes (Mounjaro). Liraglutide is approved as Saxenda and Victoza. Retatrutide, mazdutide and survodutide are investigational: phase 3 trials are running, and none of them is an approved medicine. Approval in one country does not mean approval in another. Side effects. The most common are nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting and constipation, usually early in treatment and while the amount is being increased. The labels also warn about gallbladder problems, pancreatitis, and dehydration from vomiting or diarrhoea. Resting heart rate rose by a few beats per minute in trials. Fast weight loss can include a meaningful share of muscle and other lean tissue, which is why guidance stresses protein and strength training. Stopping treatment. In a STEP 1 extension, people who stopped semaglutide regained about two-thirds of the lost weight within a year. Obesity behaves like a long-term condition, and these medicines work while they are taken. Online "research" versions. Products sold as "research use only" are not the medicines tested in trials. Nobody checks their identity, amount, purity or sterility, and the FDA has warned about counterfeit and unapproved versions. For retatrutide, which is approved nowhere, any product sold to the public is outside the trials. Every medicine in this guide has its own card in the PepSafe catalog with status, mechanism, evidence and sources, and the comparison pages set them side by side. Educational content, not medical advice: decisions about treatment belong with a doctor who knows your case. t: KLOW 80: what is in the vial and what we don't know
x: KLOW is a blend of four peptides in one vial: GHK-Cu , BPC-157 , TB-500 and KPV. The 80 is the total mass in milligrams. Sellers usually list 50 mg GHK-Cu and 10 mg each of BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV, but ratios vary between makers and nobody checks them independently. KLOW is essentially the GLOW blend (GHK-Cu, BPC-157, TB-500) plus KPV. Neither the blend nor any of its ingredients is an approved drug. No clinical trial of KLOW as a whole has been published. For the ingredients, evidence comes mostly from cell cultures and animal studies. For BPC-157, a 2025 review found only 3 small human studies, under 30 people in total, without control groups. Seller claims such as faster healing, regeneration and less inflammation are animal results carried over to people, not clinical data. Nobody has studied how the four substances act together: whether they add up, cancel out or cause new side effects. Concrete risks: a “research only” product does not have to meet drug standards for sterility and purity, so the vial may hold a different amount than labelled, impurities or endotoxins. Injecting a non-sterile solution risks infection. BPC-157 and TB-500 affect blood vessel growth, which could in theory matter with cancer. BPC-157 and TB-500 are on the WADA prohibited list. Legal status: in July 2026 an FDA advisory committee backed adding BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV to the list of substances pharmacies may compound. That is not drug approval, the FDA has not decided yet, and it does not cover ready-made blends from online shops. We give no KLOW dose, because none has been established in humans. Numbers online are guesswork. t: Peptides in cosmetics: studies versus marketing
x: Manufacturers usually split cosmetic peptides into signal peptides (meant to prompt skin cells to make collagen), carrier peptides such as copper-binding GHK-Cu , and neuromodulating ones such as acetyl hexapeptide-8, marketed as “Botox in a cream”. The catch is that much of the evidence comes from lab work, animal studies or small manufacturer-sponsored trials. A review describing GHK-Cu credits it with antioxidant and regenerative effects but rests mostly on in vitro and animal studies. Large molecules struggle to cross the epidermis, so formulation matters. It is reasonable to judge results after several weeks of regular use, not expect a clinic-level change, and patch-test on a small area of skin. t: “Research use only” peptides: why they are a bad idea
x: Peptides labelled “for laboratory research only”, such as BPC-157 , are sold online. Many are not approved as drugs. Such products need not meet drug manufacturing standards, so contents, purity, strength and sterility are hard to verify. Human data are very thin. A 2025 review cited by Prof. Stuart Phillips of McMaster University found only three human studies of BPC-157, with fewer than 30 participants in total and no control groups. Animal results often fail to carry over to people, there are no established doses, and side effects from longer use may take months or years to appear. What to do instead: peptide drugs such as insulin and GLP-1 analogues have approved uses and quality control but need a doctor's decision. For injuries, rehabilitation, sleep and enough dietary protein are proven. Athletes should note that many peptides and growth factors are on the WADA prohibited list. t: The July 2026 FDA committee vote: what it really means for BPC-157 and others
x: On 22–23 July 2026 the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) reviewed seven peptides. It backed six: BPC-157 , TB-500 and KPV (each 8 to 6 with one abstention), plus MOTS-c , Semax and Epitalon . It rejected DSIP (emideltide) 6 to 7. What it means: the committee recommends adding these substances to the 503A list of bulk ingredients US pharmacies may compound on an individual prescription. The recommendation is non-binding. The FDA still has to run its own process, estimated at several months to over a year. What it does not mean: it is not drug approval. There are no phase 3 trials, established doses or indications. FDA staff raised safety and evidence concerns, and the votes were close. It applies only to US prescription compounding, not to “research” products from online shops or blends such as GLOW or KLOW . In Poland and the EU these substances are still not authorised as medicines. We will update the PepSafe catalog when the FDA makes a final decision.
